name: Store water
summary: Food-grade drums and tanks, kept dark and sealed, keep treated water for months. The overlooked stock is water already inside buildings: a tank water heater holds 100–300 litres of drinkable water, and toilet cisterns, office water coolers and pipes hold more. Treat anything of doubtful origin before drinking.

parts.why: Drums, IBC totes and tanks to hold water
Water already sitting in heaters, cisterns and coolers
A few drops keep stored water safe
Fills and drains tanks without lifting
Taps and drain valves on tanks and heaters

tips: To drain a water heater: shut off its power or gas, open a hot tap to let air in, then open the drain valve at the bottom.

Use containers made for food or water (USU water). Recycling mark 2 only means HDPE, which also makes bleach and laundry jugs, so it doesn't prove a container is food-safe (USU plastics). Never reuse ones that held chemicals or fuel (Washington DOH).
Keep stored water dark and cool, and use it up and replace it every 6 months (Washington DOH, USU water).

Toilet tank water (never the bowl) is a last resort: CDC says it can be used if it is clear and has no toilet cleaner in it (CDC find water), while Washington DOH says not to use it (Washington DOH). If you do, boil or disinfect it first.
Health Canada's emergency kit lists 2 litres of water a person a day and suggests adding 2 more for cooking and cleaning, to cover at least 72 hours (Health Canada emergency).

Sphere's daily budget per person: 2.5 to 3 L to drink (with food), 2 to 6 L for basic hygiene and 3 to 6 L for cooking, 7.5 to 15 L in all; 15 L is the usual minimum (Sphere). Very hot weather and hard work can double a person's needs (Washington DOH).
Don't pour used water away: Alberta says to use non-potable water to flush a toilet, by filling a bucket and pouring it straight into the bowl (Alberta water shortages).
